items.title: A Philosopher on Luck
items.tvi: Nhà triết học bàn về may mắn
items.text: We tend to judge people by what they do, but a moment's reflection reveals how much of what they do is shaped by circumstances beyond their control. Philosophers call this moral luck. Consider two drivers who, after a party, each drive home having had a glass too many. One arrives safely; the other, through no greater fault of his own, encounters a child who has run into the road. The second driver will be prosecuted and condemned; the first will, at most, feel a twinge of guilt the next morning. Yet their choices were identical. What differed was luck. The unsettling implication is that our judgements of praise and blame are, to a considerable degree, judgements of outcome rather than intention. One might respond that we should therefore judge only intentions. But that position has its own difficulties: it would require us to treat the careless driver who kills a child exactly as we treat the careless driver who gets home safely, and very few people find that intuitively acceptable. The problem, in other words, is not easily resolved. Perhaps the most we can do is to remain aware of it, and to temper our condemnation of others with the recognition that, but for circumstance, we might have stood where they stand.

qs.q: What point does the example of the two drivers illustrate?
qs.a: Identical choices can be judged differently because of outcomes
w: Drinking and driving is always punished
One driver was more careful than the other

qs.q: Why does the speaker reject judging only intentions?
qs.a: Most people would find the result hard to accept

qs.q: What does the speaker suggest in the final sentence?
qs.a: We should be more modest in blaming others

items.title: Two Critics Debate a Novel
items.tvi: Hai nhà phê bình tranh luận về một cuốn tiểu thuyết
lines: I'll be blunt: I found the novel insufferably self-indulgent. Six hundred pages, and the plot could be summarised on a postcard.
But surely plot isn't the point. It's a novel about consciousness, about the texture of a single day. Complaining that nothing happens is rather like complaining that a symphony has no dialogue.
That's a seductive comparison, but a symphony doesn't ask for twenty hours of my time. At some point the reader is entitled to ask what all this attentiveness is in service of.
I'd argue it's in service of attentiveness itself. We spend our lives skimming. A book that forces us to slow down and notice is doing something genuinely countercultural.
Countercultural, perhaps. Enjoyable, rarely. I kept feeling that the author was more interested in demonstrating his sensitivity than in sharing it.
Now that's a fairer criticism, and I'll concede there are passages that tip into showing off. But the final chapter, the mother at the window, redeemed all of it for me.
I'll grant you the final chapter. I just wish I hadn't had to wade through five hundred pages to reach it.

qs.q: What is the man's main complaint about the novel?
qs.a: It is very long but has little story

qs.q: How does the woman defend the book?
qs.a: It makes readers slow down and pay attention
w: It is shorter than most novels

qs.q: What do the two critics finally agree on?
qs.a: The last chapter is excellent
w: The author is showing off throughout

items.title: A Talk on the History of Timekeeping
items.tvi: Bài nói về lịch sử đo thời gian
items.text: It's easy to assume that people have always lived by the clock, but standardised time is a remarkably recent invention. Until the mid-nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, set by the position of the sun. When it was noon in one city, it might be several minutes earlier or later in another just a short distance away. For most purposes this hardly mattered. What changed everything was the railway. Trains travelling between towns with different local times made timetables a nightmare, and collisions a genuine danger. British railway companies began adopting a single standard time in the 1840s, and by the 1880s the idea of dividing the world into time zones had been agreed internationally. Not everyone welcomed it. Some local communities resented what they saw as an imposition by distant authorities, and a few clocks were deliberately kept showing both local and railway time. Historians have argued that standard time did more than coordinate trains: it changed how people experienced their days, subordinating the natural rhythm of sunrise and sunset to the requirements of industry and commerce.

qs.q: How did towns set their time before standardisation?
qs.a: By the position of the sun

qs.q: Why did the railways need standard time?
qs.a: Different local times caused confusion and danger

qs.q: What broader effect of standard time do historians mention?
qs.a: People's days became organised around industry, not nature

items.title: Interview with an Economist
items.tvi: Phỏng vấn nhà kinh tế
lines: Your new book argues that economic growth, as conventionally measured, tells us surprisingly little about wellbeing. Isn't that a rather fashionable position?

It's become fashionable, which is not the same as being wrong. GDP measures the value of goods and services exchanged in the market. It counts the money spent cleaning up after a disaster as a positive contribution, while ignoring entirely the unpaid work of caring for children or elderly relatives. It was never designed to measure how well people's lives are going, and its inventor said so explicitly.
But growth has lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Surely that matters?

Enormously, and I'd never dismiss it. Below a certain level of income, growth and wellbeing move very closely together. My argument concerns richer societies, where the relationship weakens considerably. Beyond that point, things like health, security, the quality of relationships and a sense of purpose seem to matter at least as much as additional income.
So what would you have governments do, abandon GDP?

Not abandon it, supplement it. Several countries now publish wellbeing dashboards alongside conventional figures. The danger isn't that we measure growth; it's that we treat it as the only thing worth measuring.

qs.q: What is one weakness of GDP mentioned by the economist?
qs.a: It ignores unpaid caring work

qs.q: When does the economist say growth and wellbeing are closely linked?
qs.a: In poorer societies

qs.q: What does the economist recommend?
qs.a: Using other measures alongside GDP

items.title: A Lecture on Memory and Testimony
items.tvi: Bài giảng về trí nhớ và lời khai
items.text: Courts have long placed great weight on eyewitness testimony, and juries in particular find a confident witness extraordinarily persuasive. Yet decades of research have shown that memory is not a recording but a reconstruction, assembled anew each time we recall an event and vulnerable to influence at every stage. In a classic series of experiments, participants who watched film of a car accident were later asked how fast the cars were going when they either 'hit' or 'smashed into' each other. Those who heard the word 'smashed' gave higher estimates of speed and, a week later, were more than twice as likely to report having seen broken glass, although there was none. Equally troubling is the relationship between confidence and accuracy. A witness's confidence often grows over time, especially if they receive feedback suggesting they identified the right person, while the accuracy of their memory does not. By the time of the trial, a witness who was initially hesitant may testify with complete certainty. None of this implies that witnesses are dishonest. The point is that sincerity and reliability are different things, and a justice system that conflates them is likely, sooner or later, to convict the innocent.

qs.q: How does the speaker describe memory?
qs.a: As something rebuilt each time we remember

qs.q: What happened to participants who heard 'smashed'?
qs.a: They later remembered glass that wasn't there

qs.q: What is the speaker's main warning?
qs.a: An honest witness is not necessarily an accurate one

items.title: Colleagues Discuss Artificial Intelligence at Work
items.tvi: Đồng nghiệp bàn về trí tuệ nhân tạo trong công việc
lines: Have you tried the new drafting tool the firm's introduced? It produced a perfectly respectable contract in about thirty seconds.

I have, and that's precisely what worries me. Not that it's bad, but that it's good enough. Junior lawyers have always learned by drafting precisely these kinds of documents. If the machine does it, how do they ever develop judgement?
I suppose they'd learn by reviewing the machine's work instead.

Perhaps, but reviewing isn't the same as creating. You only really understand why a clause is worded a particular way when you've tried and failed to word it yourself. I worry we'll end up with a generation of lawyers who can spot that something looks plausible without understanding why it might be wrong.
That's a fair concern, though people said much the same about calculators and maths.

They did, and to some extent they were right. Mental arithmetic did decline. The question is whether what we lose matters. With calculators, arguably not much. With legal judgement, I'm far less sure.
So you'd rather we didn't use it?
No, I'd rather we used it deliberately, and kept some tasks for people precisely because they're how expertise is formed.

qs.q: Why is the man worried about the drafting tool?
qs.a: Junior staff may not develop judgement

qs.q: What does he say about reviewing compared with creating?
qs.a: Reviewing doesn't give the same understanding

qs.q: What is his final position?
qs.a: Use the tool carefully and keep some tasks for people

items.title: A Talk on Translation and Culture
items.tvi: Bài nói về dịch thuật và văn hoá
items.text: It is sometimes claimed that certain words are untranslatable: that the Portuguese 'saudade', for example, or the Vietnamese 'thương', capture emotions for which other languages simply have no equivalent. The claim is appealing, and it flatters the cultures concerned, but it needs careful handling. Of course no single English word corresponds exactly to 'thương', which can encompass love, pity, tenderness and a kind of protective concern. But the absence of a single word is not the same as the absence of the concept. English speakers are perfectly capable of experiencing, and describing, that cluster of feelings; they merely require a phrase rather than a word. What the existence of such terms does reveal is which experiences a culture has found important enough to lexicalise, to package into a single convenient unit. That is genuinely interesting, but it tells us about emphasis and attention rather than about the limits of human feeling. To insist otherwise is to slip towards the view that speakers of different languages inhabit sealed worlds, a view that the everyday success of translators, however imperfect, rather contradicts.

qs.q: What is the speaker's view of 'untranslatable' words?
qs.a: The idea is attractive but often exaggerated
w: Such words prove cultures cannot understand each other
Every word can be translated exactly

qs.q: What does the existence of such words reveal, according to the speaker?
qs.a: What a culture considers important

qs.q: What contradicts the 'sealed worlds' view?
qs.a: The fact that translators manage to translate

items.title: A Debate on Tourism
items.tvi: Tranh luận về du lịch
lines: The figures speak for themselves. Tourism provides millions of jobs and has transformed entire regions. To talk about restricting it is a luxury only the comfortable can afford.

Nobody's disputing the economic benefits. But you're treating tourism as a single thing, when its effects depend entirely on how it's managed. Look at towns where cruise ships unload thousands of visitors for four hours. They spend almost nothing locally, crowd out residents and leave behind rubbish and rising rents.
Those are problems of management, not of tourism itself.

Exactly my point. Which is why limits, sensibly applied, aren't anti-tourism. A cap on daily visitors, a tax that funds local services, rules on short-term rentals. These protect the very qualities that attract people in the first place.
And who decides where the cap should be? It's very easy for a city council to price out ordinary travellers while the wealthy carry on as before.
That's a legitimate risk, and I'd want any scheme designed with that in mind. But the alternative, doing nothing, has its own victims, and they're usually the people who live there.

qs.q: What is the woman's main argument at the start?
qs.a: Tourism brings important economic benefits

qs.q: What does the man say about cruise ship visitors?
qs.a: They bring problems but spend little locally
w: They spend a lot of money

qs.q: What risk of limits does the woman point out?
qs.a: They might exclude less wealthy travellers

items.title: A Scientist on Uncertainty
items.tvi: Nhà khoa học bàn về sự không chắc chắn
items.text: One of the most persistent misunderstandings between scientists and the public concerns the word 'theory'. In everyday speech, a theory is a guess, a hunch that may or may not be correct. In science, it means something closer to the opposite: a well-substantiated explanation that has survived repeated attempts to disprove it. When a scientist says that evolution is 'only a theory', she is not expressing doubt; she is placing it in the same category as the theory of gravity. Similar confusion surrounds uncertainty. Scientists are trained to state the limits of their knowledge, to attach margins of error to their estimates and to acknowledge alternative explanations. Within science, this is a mark of rigour. Outside it, it is frequently heard as weakness or evasion, and it can be exploited by those who wish to cast doubt on inconvenient findings. The solution is not for scientists to abandon caution, which would undermine the very thing that makes their conclusions trustworthy. It is rather to explain, patiently and repeatedly, that uncertainty about details is entirely compatible with confidence about the larger picture.

qs.q: What does 'theory' mean in science?
qs.a: A strongly supported explanation
w: A guess that is probably wrong

qs.q: How is scientific uncertainty often misunderstood?
qs.a: As a sign of weakness

qs.q: What does the speaker recommend scientists do?
qs.a: Explain that uncertainty about details is normal

items.title: Friends Discuss Ambition
items.tvi: Bạn bè bàn về tham vọng
lines: Do you ever feel you've settled? I look at people from university running companies and writing books, and I'm still in the same job I had ten years ago.
Actually, yes, most days. That's what makes it so confusing. I feel as though I ought to want more.
Ought according to whom, though? It sounds as if you're measuring yourself against a story about success that you've never actually chosen.
Maybe. But isn't a bit of ambition healthy? Otherwise we'd all just stagnate.

Of course, but ambition for what? There's a difference between wanting to get better at something you care about and wanting to look successful to people you barely know. The first tends to make people happier; the second rarely does, because there's always someone further ahead.
So you think I should stop comparing myself?
I think you should notice when you're doing it, and ask whether the comparison tells you anything you actually want to know.

qs.q: Why is the woman confused about her feelings?
qs.a: She enjoys her job but thinks she should want more
w: She wants to start a company

qs.q: Which kind of ambition does the man think leads to happiness?
qs.a: Wanting to improve at something you care about

qs.q: What does the man advise?
qs.a: Be aware of comparisons and question their value

items.title: A Discussion on Translating Poetry
items.tvi: Bàn về dịch thơ
lines: You've translated poetry from Vietnamese into English for twenty years. Is it even possible?

It depends what you mean by possible. If you mean producing an English poem that does exactly what the original does, then no, never. The sound of Vietnamese, the tones, the way meaning shifts with a single syllable, none of that survives. What you can do is make choices about what matters most in a particular poem and try to keep that.
How do you decide what matters most?

I read the poem dozens of times, often aloud, until I have a sense of where its energy lies. Sometimes it's an image, sometimes a rhythm, sometimes a kind of ironic distance. Then I'm prepared to sacrifice almost everything else to preserve it. Readers occasionally write to complain that I've added words or changed a metaphor, and they're right, I have. But a translation that is faithful to every word and dead on the page betrays the poet far more seriously.
The living ones usually understand. Some even prefer the freer versions. It's the scholars who tend to be more upset.

qs.q: What does the translator say cannot be preserved in translation?
qs.a: The sound and tonal qualities of Vietnamese
w: The general meaning of the poem

qs.q: How does she decide what to preserve?
qs.a: By identifying the poem's central quality through repeated reading
w: By following strict rules of translation

qs.q: How does she respond to readers' complaints?
qs.a: She accepts their observation but defends her approach
w: She says they have misunderstood the original
She promises to change her translations

qs.q: What does she imply about scholars?
qs.a: They are often more concerned with literal accuracy than poets are

items.title: A Talk on the Economics of Attention
items.tvi: Bài nói về kinh tế học của sự chú ý
items.text: Economists usually study scarce resources: land, labour, capital. I want to suggest that in wealthy, connected societies, the scarcest resource of all may be attention. Information is now so abundant that the limiting factor is no longer access to it but our capacity to process it. And wherever there is scarcity, there is a market. Much of the digital economy can be understood as a competition to capture and sell human attention, usually to advertisers. This has consequences that are easy to overlook. Products that are free to the user are rarely free in any meaningful sense; we pay for them with time and with data about our behaviour, and the companies involved have strong incentives to design services that are difficult to put down. That is not necessarily sinister, but it does mean that the interests of the user and the interests of the provider are not always aligned. Some economists have proposed that attention be treated rather like pollution: a shared resource that markets tend to overexploit unless there are rules. I'm not entirely persuaded by that analogy, since attention, unlike clean air, is individual as well as collective. But I do think the comparison is useful in one respect. It reminds us that what is rational for each company may not be good for society as a whole.

qs.q: What is the speaker's central claim?
qs.a: Attention has become an extremely scarce resource
w: Information is becoming harder to access

qs.q: What does the speaker say about “free” digital products?
qs.a: Users pay with their time and personal data
w: They are paid for by governments
They are genuinely free of cost

qs.q: What is the speaker's attitude to the comparison with pollution?
qs.a: Partly unconvinced but sees some value in it

qs.q: What lesson does the speaker draw from the comparison?
qs.a: Individual business decisions may harm society overall
w: Attention should be taxed like pollution

items.title: A Panel on Ageing Populations
items.tvi: Tọa đàm về dân số già
lines: Many countries in Asia are ageing faster than Europe ever did. Is this a crisis?

I'm wary of the word crisis. Longer lives are, after all, one of humanity's great achievements. The challenge is that our institutions, pensions, health systems, even the design of our cities, were built for a population with far more young people than old. They need to adapt, and quickly.

Several things. Raising retirement ages gradually, which is politically unpopular but probably unavoidable. Making it easier for older people to keep working part time if they wish. And investing in prevention, so that people stay healthy for longer rather than simply living longer with illness.
Some argue that immigration is the answer.

It can help, certainly, and in some sectors, like elderly care, it already does. But it's not a complete solution. Migrants also age, and many of the countries they come from are ageing too. Relying on immigration alone would simply postpone the problem.

qs.q: Why does the speaker avoid the word “crisis”?
qs.a: Longer life expectancy is a positive development
w: The problem has already been solved

qs.q: What does she say about raising the retirement age?
qs.a: It is unpopular but likely to be necessary
w: It should be avoided at all costs
It will solve the problem by itself

qs.q: What is the aim of investing in prevention, according to her?
qs.a: Helping people stay healthy as they age

qs.q: What is her view of immigration as a solution?
qs.a: Useful but only a partial and temporary answer

items.title: An Author on Writing Historical Fiction
items.tvi: Nhà văn nói về viết tiểu thuyết lịch sử
items.text: People often ask me how much of my novels is true, and I've come to think the question, though perfectly reasonable, slightly misunderstands what historical fiction does. I do an enormous amount of research. For my last book, set in Hue in the 1880s, I spent two years reading letters, court records and travellers' accounts, and I was scrupulous about the events that are documented. But the documents tell you what happened, not what it felt like, and they almost never tell you anything about the people who weren't powerful enough to leave records. That silence is where the novelist works. When I invent a cook in the palace kitchen, or a boatman on the Perfume River, I'm not claiming that person existed. I'm trying to imagine, as responsibly as I can, a kind of life the archives ignore. There's a risk, of course. Readers may come away believing that something I invented is historical fact, and I take that seriously. That's why I include a note at the end of each book separating what is documented from what is imagined. Some readers find it spoils the illusion. I think they're owed it.

qs.q: Why does the author think the question about truth is slightly misguided?
qs.a: Historical fiction aims to imagine what documents cannot show
w: Her novels contain no real events
Readers are not interested in history

qs.q: What does she say about her treatment of documented events?
qs.a: She is careful to represent them accurately
w: She changes them to improve the story

qs.q: Why does she invent characters such as the cook and the boatman?
qs.a: To represent people who left no historical records
w: Because real historical figures are boring

qs.q: What is her attitude towards the note at the end of her books?
qs.a: She believes readers deserve it, even if some dislike it

items.title: Colleagues Discuss a Difficult Decision
items.tvi: Đồng nghiệp bàn về một quyết định khó
lines: Have you heard the board wants to close the Da Nang office?
I heard rumours. Is it definite?
Not yet, but the figures don't look good. It's been losing money for three years.

I'm not sure the figures tell the whole story, though. That office brings in most of our clients from the central region, even if the revenue gets recorded here in Hanoi. If we close it, I suspect we'll lose more than we save.
That's an interesting point. Has anyone put that to the board?
I doubt it. The report they're working from only looks at each office's own accounts. It's the kind of analysis that's technically correct and practically misleading.
Then perhaps we should put together a short paper showing where those clients actually come from.
I'd be willing to do that, but I'd rather it came from both of us. If I do it alone, it'll look as though I'm just protecting my old team.
Fair enough. Let's work on it together.

qs.q: Why is the board considering closing the office?
qs.a: It has been unprofitable for several years
w: Its staff want to move to Hanoi

qs.q: What does the man believe about the financial figures?
qs.a: They do not show the office's full contribution
w: They are completely accurate and complete

qs.q: What does he mean by “technically correct and practically misleading”?
qs.a: The analysis is accurate but leads to the wrong conclusion
w: The analysis is too difficult to understand

qs.q: Why does he want the paper to come from both of them?
qs.a: He is worried it will seem self-interested otherwise
w: He does not have time to write it
The woman knows more about the clients

items.title: A Lecture on the Psychology of Risk
items.tvi: Bài giảng về tâm lý học của rủi ro
items.text: Ask people which is more dangerous, flying or driving, and most will correctly say driving. Yet many of those same people feel far more anxious on an aircraft than behind the wheel. This gap between what we know and what we feel is central to the psychology of risk. Several factors seem to inflate our sense of danger. Risks we cannot control feel worse than those we can, which is partly why passengers fear flying while drivers, with their hands on the wheel, tend to feel safe. Risks that are dramatic and memorable, such as a plane crash or a shark attack, loom larger than those that accumulate quietly, such as a poor diet. And unfamiliar risks unsettle us more than familiar ones, even when the familiar ones kill far more people. None of this makes us simply irrational. These intuitions evolved in a world in which vivid, unfamiliar and uncontrollable dangers were often genuinely the most threatening. The difficulty is that modern statistics and ancient instincts frequently point in different directions, and public policy, which responds to fear as much as to evidence, is pulled between the two.

qs.q: Why does the lecturer compare flying and driving?
qs.a: To show that feelings about risk differ from knowledge
w: To prove that flying is more dangerous
To explain why people prefer driving

qs.q: According to the lecturer, why do drivers tend to feel safe?
qs.a: They feel in control

qs.q: What is the lecturer's view of our intuitions about risk?
qs.a: They once made sense but often mislead us today
w: They are more reliable than statistics

items.title: Two Editors Discuss a Memoir
items.tvi: Hai biên tập viên bàn về một cuốn hồi ký
lines: I've finished the memoir. It's beautifully written, but I'm uneasy about the chapter on her father.
Because her brother says it didn't happen that way?
Partly. He's written to us, quite politely, saying that several of the scenes are invented. Conversations he says never took place.
Memoirists reconstruct dialogue all the time. Nobody remembers a conversation from thirty years ago word for word. Readers understand that.
Reconstructing is one thing. But if an entire episode is imagined, then surely we're publishing fiction under a false label.
Or we're publishing one person's truth, which is what a memoir has always been. Her brother's memory isn't automatically more reliable than hers.
Agreed. Still, I'd feel more comfortable with an author's note acknowledging that others remember events differently.
I could live with that, as long as it doesn't read as an apology. The book deserves better than that.

qs.q: What has the author's brother claimed?
qs.a: Some scenes in the book were made up
w: Their father wants the book withdrawn

qs.q: What is the man's view of reconstructed dialogue?
qs.a: It is normal and readers accept it
w: It is acceptable only in fiction

qs.q: What do the editors finally agree on?
qs.a: Adding a note about differing memories
w: Removing the chapter about the father
Asking the brother to write a reply

items.title: A Talk on Silence in Music
items.tvi: Bài nói về khoảng lặng trong âm nhạc
items.text: We usually think of music as sound, and silence as its absence: the empty space before the first note and after the last. But composers and performers have long known that silence is part of the material. A pause before the final chord can create more tension than any crescendo; a rest in the middle of a phrase can make the following note feel inevitable or surprising, depending on its length. The most famous experiment along these lines is John Cage's 'silent' piece, first performed in 1952, in which a pianist sits at the instrument for four minutes and thirty-three seconds without playing. Audiences were often outraged, assuming it was a joke at their expense. Cage's point, however, was more subtle: there is no such thing as true silence. The 'silence' of the piece is filled with coughs, rain on the roof and the creak of seats, sounds that we normally filter out. Whether one regards the piece as profound or as a provocation, it does something few concerts manage: it makes the audience listen to everything.

qs.q: What point does the speaker make about pauses in music?
qs.a: They can build tension and shape what follows
w: They are mainly for performers to rest
They matter less than loud passages

qs.q: How did audiences often react to Cage's piece?
qs.a: They thought they were being mocked
w: They asked for it to be repeated

qs.q: What was Cage's real point, according to the speaker?
qs.a: True silence does not exist

items.title: Interview with an Urban Planner
items.tvi: Phỏng vấn nhà quy hoạch đô thị
lines: You've said that building more roads doesn't reduce traffic. That sounds counter-intuitive.

It does, but the evidence is remarkably consistent. When you add road capacity, journeys initially get faster, so more people choose to drive, at more times of day, and within a few years congestion is back where it started. Planners call it induced demand.
So what's the alternative? Simply letting traffic grind to a halt?

Not at all. The alternative is to give people realistic choices. If a bus is frequent and reliable, or a cycle route is safe, a proportion of drivers will switch, and that frees up the road for those who genuinely need it. Delivery vans, for instance.
Critics would say that's social engineering.

Every transport decision is social engineering. A six-lane motorway shapes behaviour just as much as a cycle lane does. The question isn't whether we influence how people travel, because we always do. It's which outcomes we're choosing.

qs.q: According to the planner, what happens when road capacity is increased?
qs.a: Traffic eventually returns to its earlier level

qs.q: What alternative does the planner propose?
qs.a: Offering good alternatives to driving

qs.q: How does he respond to the charge of 'social engineering'?
qs.a: All transport decisions influence behaviour
w: He admits that it is a danger
He says planners should avoid it

items.title: A Radio Essay on Handwriting
items.tvi: Tiểu luận trên đài về chữ viết tay
items.text: When did you last write a letter by hand? For many of us, handwriting has shrunk to shopping lists and signatures, and some schools have reduced the time spent teaching it. Is anything lost? The evidence is more interesting than either nostalgists or enthusiasts for technology tend to admit. Several studies suggest that students who take notes by hand remember lectures somewhat better than those who type, perhaps because writing is slower and forces them to summarise rather than transcribe. Other researchers have failed to replicate the effect, or have found it to be small. What seems clearer is that learning to form letters by hand helps young children recognise them: the movement of the hand appears to reinforce the shape in memory. Beyond the research, there is something harder to measure. A handwritten note carries traces of its writer: hurry, care, hesitation, a crossing-out. Perhaps that is why, in an age of instant messages, a handwritten card can still feel like a small act of generosity. It costs the sender time, and time, these days, is what we value most.

qs.q: Why might handwritten notes help students remember?
qs.a: Writing slowly forces them to summarise
w: Handwriting is easier to read later

qs.q: What does the speaker say about the research on note-taking?
qs.a: Its findings have not always been confirmed
w: It proves that typing is harmful
It has only studied young children

qs.q: Why, according to the speaker, can a handwritten card feel generous?
qs.a: It shows the sender has given up time
w: It is more expensive than a message
It is easier to keep than a message
